Then I draw alert evaluation as its own consumer, rather than a dashboard request that happens to run repeatedly. The catalog beside ingress explains how a label explosion is stopped before it becomes storage debt.

`POST /samples` sends a bounded batch containing tenant-scoped labels, timestamps and producer sequence IDs; acknowledgement follows durable log replication. Workers dedupe, sort bounded late arrivals and write immutable blocks with manifests. Late data rewrites a versioned block or adds a correction block under a stated lateness cutoff.

`GET /query?metric=latency&window=1h&step=60s` selects matching series, fans out only to their shards and merges statistics at the requested resolution. A fresh tail covers the interval not yet compacted. Alerts evaluate a short recent window on reserved capacity. The evaluator records pending/firing/resolved state and writes notification intents durably so restarts do not lose a page.

A query response contains `{resolution:"60s", series:[...], as_of:"...", partial:false}`. Exceeding the scan budget returns a clear limit error or explicitly partial result; it never silently presents an incomplete aggregate as complete.
references.failure:
When ingestion doubles to ten million samples/s during an incident, I protect critical health metrics with reserved capacity and per-tenant admission. Agents use bounded buffers and retry only unacknowledged batches. If we must drop, I expose dropped counts and a gap marker; I do not acknowledge data that was discarded as if it were durable. Sampling counters or histogram data needs an explicit estimator, not arbitrary deletion.

When a region stops reporting I mark its series stale or unknown and evaluate a reporting-health rule using expected reporters and an independent heartbeat source. A threshold expression on an absent series must not become a successful zero-value measurement. Alerts can enter no-data separately from firing; the policy decides whether that pages.

Storage-worker loss replays from the log and publishes block manifests conditionally. Evaluator failover preserves rule state and uses an epoch plus stable notification transition IDs. Alert delivery is still at least once, so the receiver deduplicates. During backlog I show query freshness and ensure old samples do not trigger a misleading 'healthy now' result.
references.ops:
I would monitor ingest lag, compaction lag, new-series rate, cardinality rejections, dropped samples, query scanned-series count and alert evaluation age. An external watchdog observes evaluator heartbeats and notification delivery; the alerting service cannot be its own only alarm. The breach-to-notification budget includes ingest delay, evaluation interval and downstream delivery, not just expression execution.

A rule state machine starts inactive, becomes pending for a configured duration, then firing, and resolves after a recovery threshold or grace interval. Hysteresis prevents a value near a threshold from paging repeatedly. Notification keys identify rule, tenant and state transition; retrying an outbox entry keeps that key.

I would test a disappearing region, delayed samples, counter resets and a high-cardinality tenant. Histogram quantiles use merged bucket counts, following the distinction between summaries and histograms in [Prometheus documentation](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/histograms/). Rollup jobs retain raw evidence until replacement blocks are verified. Query cost limits and tenant fairness keep one broad dashboard from consuming the evaluator's thirty-second budget.

probes.question: What does HTTP 200 mean for your delivery guarantee?
probes.answer: HTTP 200 means the endpoint acknowledged our attempt. It does not prove exactly-once business processing. The receiver should durably commit or enqueue before returning 2xx and dedupe by stable event ID. If it processes but the response times out, we retry that same event with a fresh timestamp/signature, so duplicate delivery is expected.

probes.question: How do you avoid one slow tenant blocking everyone?
probes.answer: Each endpoint has inflight, rate and retry-budget limits, with separate scheduling shares from healthy first attempts. Hard timeouts free sockets, and a circuit breaker delays repeated failures without dropping durable deliveries. After recovery I drain gradually. One slow tenant cannot borrow unlimited workers merely because its queue is large.

probes.question: How do you safely deliver to arbitrary customer URLs?
probes.answer: An enforced egress proxy validates schemes, ports, DNS answers, IPv4/IPv6 ranges and redirects, then connects only to the validated destination with TLS hostname checks. I block internal, link-local and metadata targets, cap response size and set timeouts. Revalidating at connection time is necessary for DNS rebinding; a one-time URL check is insufficient.

probes.question: Work out the retry budget: how many attempts fit in the 24-hour window, and what happens to the deliveries that run out?
probes.answer: At 100 million events a day that is about 1,157 events/s, and at the maximum twenty subscribers, 1,157 x 20 = 23,148 first attempts a second before any retry. The 24-hour window is a count cap as well as a clock: I set twelve automatic attempts, so a delivery that fails every time is attempted twelve times in its life and never a thirteenth, which bounds amplification at 23,148 x 12 = 277,778 attempts a second instead of the orders of magnitude a bare exponential curve suggests. With a 60-second base delay doubling to a one-hour cap, the eleven waits are 60, 120, 240, 480, 960, 1,920, 3,600, 3,600, 3,600, 3,600 seconds, which is 21,780 seconds or about 6 hours, so the count cap binds well before the clock for a destination failing immediately. The 24 hours is what catches the sparse case, one failure every few hours. Deliveries that reach twelve attempts or pass 24 hours enter a visible dead-letter state and are replayable, never dropped, and a replay opens a fresh budget against the same immutable event.

probes.question: Is the subscriber URL validated once at subscribe time or on every attempt, and what does a DNS change do to attempts in flight?
probes.answer: Both, and they do different jobs. At subscribe time I validate scheme, port and host string and record an endpoint revision, so an obviously unusable URL is rejected before any event exists for it. At every attempt the egress proxy resolves the host, checks the returned addresses against private, loopback, link-local and metadata ranges in IPv4 and IPv6, and connects only to the address it just validated, so a host that starts resolving to 169.254.169.254 after subscribe is refused at that attempt. A DNS change moves future attempts, not in-flight ones: an established connection keeps talking to the old address until it closes, and a request already sent and timing out may still land on the old host, which is part of why the signature timestamp bounds how long an old answer can matter. I record the resolved address on each attempt so an incident can tell a hijack from a misconfiguration.

failures.scenario: A popular destination is down for 12 hours.
failures.expected: I isolate endpoint concurrency, apply capped exponential backoff with jitter and preserve each delivery until its twenty-four-hour deadline. At 100 events/s, twelve hours creates 4.32 million pending deliveries in the worked example. Recovery drains at a controlled rate. Exhausted entries are inspectable and replayable; other subscribers keep their independent progress.

failures.scenario: A customer rotates their signing secret during a retry wave.
failures.expected: Each new attempt uses the currently active signing-key version and records that version, while keeping event identity stable. Normal rotation permits a bounded old/new verification overlap; already sent old-key requests may still arrive. Emergency compromise can revoke old verification immediately, accepting failures for those inflight attempts. I do not pin pending deliveries to the old secret forever.

failures.scenario: Every destination subscribed to one event type is down at the same time.
failures.expected: The backlog grows at the full delivery rate rather than the event rate: 100 million events a day is about 1,157/s, and at the assumed twenty subscribers on that event type, 1,157 x 20 = 23,148 deliveries a second, so twelve hours of outage queues 23,148 x 43,200 = 1 billion deliveries. At an assumed 1KB per scheduling record that is about 1TB of pending state, and at the twelve-attempt cap the fleet would be spending 23,148 x 12 = 277,778 attempts a second against endpoints that are all refusing. I cap the fleet inflight budget, open the circuit breaker per endpoint after a threshold, and stop minting new attempts rather than burning the fleet on a known-dead destination. Pending deliveries keep their 24-hour deadlines, so the oldest expire into a visible dead-letter state mid-outage and need an operator replay, which is why I would let an operator extend a deadline when the destination is verifiably external.

references.scope:
I would offer subscription management, event publication, delivery status, retry and authorized replay. A published event is durable; each event/subscription pair has an independent delivery outcome. The first attempt should begin within five seconds and automatic retries continue for twenty-four hours. Ordering across subscriptions is outside this contract. If a subscriber needs per-resource ordering, that requires a separate queue and head-of-line blocking policy.

The guarantee is at least once. A subscriber may process an event and lose the HTTP response, so a timeout triggers another attempt with the same event identity. A 2xx means the subscriber acknowledged receipt, not that I can prove its business transaction committed. I would document that receivers durably enqueue or commit before responding and deduplicate event IDs themselves.

I include authentication, signing, tenant authorization and controlled outbound networking. Subscribers are third-party code, so slow requests, DNS changes, secret rotation and poison endpoints are expected operating conditions, not exceptional assumptions.
references.estimates:
100 million events/day is about 1,157 events/s. At the maximum twenty subscriptions, that is two billion logical deliveries/day, around 23,148/s before retries. I will assume average fanout is four for a normal baseline of about 4,630 deliveries/s, while capacity and quotas account for the maximum separately.

Assuming a two-second mean HTTP attempt, baseline in-flight concurrency is about 9,260, and maximum-fanout concurrency is 46,296. With a five-second timeout under widespread failure, the maximum rate can hold 115,740 sockets. These numbers justify per-endpoint concurrency caps and a bounded fleet-wide inflight budget. I would not let a slow destination consume the entire worker pool.

For a popular endpoint receiving an assumed 100 events/s, twelve hours down accumulates 4.32 million deliveries. At 1KB scheduling metadata each, that is 4.32GB before attempt history. A capped policy of twelve automatic attempts in twenty-four hours bounds amplification to twelve per logical delivery; exponential backoff does not inherently create orders of magnitude of attempts. Recovery needs rate-limited catch-up so the destination is not immediately knocked down again.
references.data:
Events use `(tenant_id, event_id)` with immutable payload bytes, type, occurrence time and payload hash. Publication snapshots the eligible subscription IDs or a subscription revision, so changes do not unpredictably alter historical fanout. Each delivery is keyed by `(event_id, subscription_id)` and stores due time, state, retry deadline, endpoint revision and attempt count.

Attempts have attempt ID, start/end, outcome, HTTP status, timestamp and signing-key version. I choose the active signing key at attempt time; pending delivery records do not pin an old secret forever. Rotation keeps a bounded overlap of old/new verification keys at the subscriber, while each actual attempt records exactly which version signed its bytes. An emergency compromise can revoke the old key immediately and let new attempts use the new version.

Secrets live encrypted in a dedicated secret store. I never log them or unbounded response bodies. A stable delivery/event ID lets the subscriber dedupe despite fresh timestamps/signatures. Manual replay creates audited attempt records against the same immutable event, with a replay ID and reason; repeating the replay request uses its own client idempotency key.

Whiteboard walkthrough: I draw one event expanding into independent delivery records, then draw the retry loop around a delivery rather than event publication. The key lookup belongs to each attempt. I put the egress proxy before the customer endpoint to explain why arbitrary URLs cannot bypass address controls.

`POST /events` returns `{event_id:"e9", accepted:true}` after event and fanout intent commit. A worker claims a due delivery, resolves the approved endpoint, loads its current secret version, and sends the exact payload bytes with headers such as `Event-Id: e9`, `Signature-Version: k2` and a fresh timestamped HMAC.

A 2xx marks delivery acknowledged. Network timeout or retryable status records failure and schedules a jittered next attempt until its deadline/budget; most permanent 4xx go directly to operator-visible failure under a documented status policy. A replay API adds attempts to the recorded event/subscription pair and retains event identity. Leases fence scheduler writes, though a stalled worker can still cause duplicate HTTP delivery.

A destination down for twelve hours receives exponentially spaced attempts capped by count and twenty-four-hour age. Its independent endpoint concurrency, retry share and circuit-breaker state keep healthy subscribers moving. At recovery I drain due work gradually and respect Retry-After within policy bounds. Exhausted deliveries enter a visible dead-letter state with replay controls.

Rotation happens at the attempt boundary. New attempts use the new active key version and a fresh timestamp; already sent attempts may have used the old version. I publish overlap instructions so the receiver accepts both during ordinary rotation, then ends the overlap after the bounded in-flight interval. I record the key version in each attempt, so debugging does not confuse payload identity with signature identity. Pinning the old key on every pending delivery would make emergency revocation ineffective.

An ambiguous timeout preserves the same event ID. It may repeat a completed business effect unless the receiver deduplicates. Endpoint changes require a versioned policy: pending deliveries follow the current approved endpoint only if that is the tenant's stated choice. A malicious redirect or DNS rebinding attempt is denied by the egress layer.
references.ops:
I would monitor first-attempt lag, oldest delivery, attempt amplification, endpoint success rates, timeout sockets and dead-letter growth. Fleet averages hide one large destination, so top endpoint backlog and inflight counts are first-class. Status exposes attempts and response summaries without leaking signing material.

For SSRF I allow only approved HTTP schemes and ports, reject private/link-local/loopback and metadata addresses in IPv4 and IPv6, validate every DNS resolution and redirect, and enforce the resolved destination at connection time through the egress proxy. A URL string blocklist alone does not stop rebinding. TLS validates the intended hostname, outbound response size is capped, and there is a hard timeout.

I document receiver dedupe, signature verification over exact bytes, timestamp tolerance and key overlap. [Stripe's webhook documentation](https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks) provides a concrete reference for retry ambiguity, fresh attempt signatures and overlapping secret rotation. I would test timeout-after-processing, twelve-hour downtime and rotation with retries in progress. Replay permissions and subscription changes have an audit trail.

probes.question: What transaction prevents two simultaneous overlapping bookings?
probes.answer: A database transaction inserts the confirmed half-open timestamp range under a room/time exclusion constraint. Concurrent overlaps cannot both commit; one returns 409. A unique start time is insufficient because overlapping bookings can start at different times. Search caches and UI checks do not participate in authorization to confirm.

probes.question: How are recurring events represented and exceptions handled?
probes.answer: I retain the wall-clock start, IANA zone, recurrence rule, DST policy and expansion horizon, then materialize concrete UTC occurrences. Exceptions reference the original local occurrence identity and record cancellation or replacement. Already confirmed rows remain explicit. An infinite rule does not reserve infinitely many room slots; the UI shows the confirmed horizon.

probes.question: How do you make a retried booking request safe?
probes.answer: The tenant-scoped client key, normalized body hash and result IDs commit with the booking. Retrying the same body/key returns that result even if the first response was lost. A different body conflicts. Concurrent duplicates serialize on the unique key, while the room-range exclusion constraint handles different requests competing for the same interval.

failures.scenario: Two users book the same slot simultaneously.
failures.expected: Both search results may say free. The authoritative room/time exclusion constraint allows only one overlapping confirmed transaction to commit and returns 409 to the other. I never authorize from the stale projection. The winner's idempotency mapping and confirmation event commit together, so a lost response can be retried safely.

failures.scenario: A daylight-saving transition changes a recurring meeting time.
failures.expected: A weekly 9am series is stored as local wall time plus zone and generated separately for each date. UTC instants change across DST while 9am local remains stable. Nonexistent and ambiguous times use the explicit reject/shift/fold policy. Exceptions and confirmed occurrences retain their identities; storing one UTC timestamp plus seven-day increments would drift.

references.scope:
I would make 'no overlapping confirmed bookings for a room' the database invariant. Availability search is a suggestion, not authorization to book. The APIs cover availability, book, reschedule, cancel and bounded recurring series. Reminders, invitations and external-calendar sync are downstream consumers, not part of the booking commit.

I would clarify whether a recurring series must succeed as a whole. For this design I support atomic booking of a bounded expansion, say ninety days, and return conflicts without partial confirmation. An unlimited recurrence is a definition plus a rolling horizon, so I cannot promise every future occurrence is reserved forever. Organization admins and booking owners have explicitly scoped cancellation rights.

A reservation is confirmed only after the overlap constraint commits. Search can remain under 200ms using briefly stale materialized availability. I would accept a 409 at booking time instead of turning a fast search cache into the source of truth. Reschedule atomically replaces the old interval so the client never loses its original booking merely because the new room was unavailable.
references.estimates:
Ten million bookings/day is about 116/s globally. Spread evenly across five million rooms, that is two bookings per room per day, but airport lounges and popular meeting rooms will be far more contended. I assume a 10× write peak of 1,160/s and twenty availability searches per completed booking, giving about 2,315 average search requests/s and 23,150 peak.

Assuming each search narrows to fifty candidate rooms, naive individual checks at peak would issue about 1.16 million room-range checks/s. I would first filter rooms by organization, capacity and equipment, then use indexed interval queries or a coarsely materialized availability bitmap to narrow further. The final write still consults authoritative intervals.

At an assumed 500 bytes of booking metadata, ten million rows/day is 5GB raw; a year is about 1.825TB before indexes and replicas. Recurrence expansion amplifies writes: a weekly series over ninety days produces about thirteen occurrences. I cap expansion size and order multi-room/series locks consistently. Average global QPS does not justify ignoring the one-room conflict hotspot.
references.data:
Rooms use `(tenant_id, room_id)` with attributes and active state. Occurrences have booking ID, room ID, owner, UTC start/end, status and series ID. Intervals are half-open `[start,end)`, allowing a 10:00 finish and 10:00 start. PostgreSQL can enforce a GiST exclusion constraint on room equality and timestamp-range overlap for confirmed rows; [range-type documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/rangetypes.html) describes that mechanism. A unique room/start pair alone is insufficient for arbitrary overlapping durations.

Series definitions retain local start time, IANA time zone, recurrence rule, duration, DST policy and expansion horizon. UTC occurrence rows are generated from that wall-clock rule. An exception key identifies the original local recurrence occurrence, with cancellation or replacement data. Storing only the first UTC timestamp would shift a weekly 9am meeting across daylight-saving changes.

Submission keys are unique `(tenant_id, idempotency_key)` and store a body hash plus the resulting booking/series IDs. Notifications use a transactional outbox. Availability indexes are rebuildable derived state. Deleted organizations cannot acquire new bookings, while retained audit rows are tombstoned according to privacy policy.
references.flow:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
 C["Booking client"] -->|search attributes and interval| S["Availability API"]
 S -->|candidate rooms| R["Room catalog"]
 S -->|cached free intervals| V["Availability projection"]
 C -->|book with client key| A["Booking API"]
 A -->|expand local recurrence| E["Recurrence engine"]
 A -->|atomic constrained insert| D["Booking database"]
 E -->|bounded UTC occurrences| D
 D -->|committed outbox| O["Change dispatcher"]
 O -->|refresh derived availability| V
 O -->|booking confirmation| N["Notification service"]
 A -->|confirmed IDs or conflict| C
```

Whiteboard walkthrough: I draw search above booking and deliberately keep its cache outside the commit. I label the database overlap constraint as the decision point. Recurrence feeds concrete UTC occurrences into that same boundary, and notifications leave only after commit. This shows why a stale search may mislead a user briefly without double-booking a room.

`GET /availability?room_type=meeting&start=...&end=...` returns candidates with an `as_of` timestamp. `POST /bookings` with `Idempotency-Key: b17` and `{room_id:"r7", start:"...", end:"..."}` inserts the identity mapping and constrained booking in one transaction. A conflict returns 409 with an alternate-search hint; success returns `{booking_id:"b9", status:"confirmed"}`.

For recurrence, I expand a bounded set using the stored time zone, insert all occurrences transactionally, and fail the whole batch if any conflicts under the chosen all-or-nothing contract. Cancellation marks the occurrence inactive and records an outbox event. Reschedule performs the old/new transition atomically. A retry after an unknown response returns the original booking rather than attempting another reservation.
references.failure:
Two users choosing the same room can both see free search results. Their insert transactions compete on the exclusion constraint; one commits and the other receives a conflict. I do not use a check-then-insert outside a transaction. A database outage stops confirmation even if the cache says free, because availability is weaker than the no-double-booking invariant.

A retry with the same idempotency key and body reads its committed outcome. Concurrent duplicate requests serialize on that unique mapping; a reused key with another body returns 409. If the first transaction aborted, there is no accepted booking to duplicate. The key must survive for the documented retry horizon.

For daylight-saving transitions I generate each occurrence in its local time zone, then compare UTC intervals. A nonexistent spring-forward time needs a stated rule, such as reject or move forward; an ambiguous fall-back time needs an explicit offset/fold choice. I would reject ambiguity by default and ask the user rather than silently move a room booking. Time-zone database changes may affect future unmaterialized occurrences, so expansion records its version and already confirmed rows do not shift invisibly.
references.ops:
I would measure search p95, authoritative booking latency, exclusion conflicts by room, deadlocks and projection lag. A high conflict rate can mean a popular room, stale search or duplicate clients; these causes require different fixes. Cache reconciliation compares projections against committed occurrence rows, and cleanup never authorizes bookings.

Recurrence tests include half-open adjacency, a spring-forward gap, a fall-back ambiguity and an exception crossing a time-zone offset change. [RFC 5545](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5545) is a reference for recurrence and exception representation, while the application still needs an explicit booking policy for DST ambiguity. Notifications and external sync dedupe by booking change version.

Organization deletion immediately disables new operations, cancels or anonymizes bookings under a documented tenant policy and sends downstream cancellation events. I retain minimal audit evidence while removing optional personal notes. Recovery rehearses a lost success response, concurrent overlapping writes and a reschedule failure. A series expansion job nearing its horizon is monitored so the product never presents unreserved future dates as confirmed.

probes.question: How do you make percentage rollout stable for a user?
probes.answer: I hash a stable subject key with environment, flag ID and a fixed rollout salt using a documented algorithm and encoding, then map to 10,000 buckets. Changing only the threshold grows the cohort without reshuffling it. SDKs share test vectors. Changing the salt intentionally rebuckets users and is an audited rollout change.

probes.question: What if an older update arrives after a newer one?
probes.answer: Every immutable snapshot has a monotonic revision. The SDK ignores lower revisions and atomically swaps complete validated snapshots. A delta applies only to its declared base revision; if the SDK missed that base, it fetches a full snapshot. Rollback publishes previous values under a newer revision, so it is not discarded as stale.

probes.question: What stronger guarantee does an emergency kill switch need?
probes.answer: Urgent push helps connected clients but cannot reach an offline process. A safety-critical feature needs a separately validated enable lease with local fail-safe expiry, or server-side authorization at the action boundary. I declare the maximum offline continuation and availability tradeoff. Clock uncertainty/restart cannot extend the lease. Ordinary flags can remain stale without carrying this stronger contract.

failures.scenario: A bad config is rolled out globally.
failures.expected: I stop expansion, publish the previous safe values under a higher revision and watch application health recover. SDKs retain validated last-known-good snapshots if a new one is malformed. Canaries limit semantic failures that schema validation cannot catch. Safety controls have independently validated logic so a bad ordinary rule cannot suppress local fail-safe behavior.

failures.scenario: Clients are disconnected for 24h.
failures.expected: Ordinary flags use the persisted validated last-known-good snapshot and defaults until a full re-sync. Safety-sensitive enabled features expire their local permission and disable after the documented lease interval. No update can reach a disconnected process. On reconnect, version gaps trigger a full snapshot, and propagation reports distinguish disconnected clients from healthy connected ones.

references.scope:
I would separate a control plane for authoring, validation, audit and rollout from a data plane that distributes immutable snapshots. SDK evaluation is a local memory read and deterministic rule execution under 1ms; it must not call the control plane per request. The service supports percentage rollouts, targeting, defaults and emergency safety controls.

The five-second propagation objective applies to healthy connected clients. I cannot promise that a disconnected client receives a new kill-switch update. Ordinary flags use a validated last-known-good snapshot while offline, with application defaults for cold start. A safety-critical feature has a different contract: its permission to remain enabled expires locally after a configured freshness lease, and the SDK falls back to disabled if it cannot refresh. That bounds offline risk at the cost of availability.

I would ask which flags genuinely need that fail-safe behavior, since disabling a cosmetic experiment during a control-plane outage is unnecessary. Secrets are outside ordinary flag snapshots; SDK clients, especially browsers, cannot be trusted to keep a bundled configuration secret.
references.estimates:
50,000 changes/day is about 0.58 changes/s. Broadcasting every change to all 500,000 clients would cause 25 billion deliveries/day, roughly 289,352/s average. With an assumed 2KB delta, that is 50TB/day. Tenant/environment subscriptions reduce this dramatically, so I would partition distribution by the actual configuration scope instead of one global channel.

Cold starts have a different shape. If 10% of clients restart in one minute and each downloads an assumed 100KB snapshot, that is 50,000 snapshots, 5GB total and around 83MB/s before protocol overhead. Versioned immutable snapshots can be cached by environment and content hash, while authenticated access limits who can read them.

Assuming twenty evaluations/s per client gives ten million local evaluations/s across the fleet, with no centralized QPS. A 1ms worst-case evaluator would consume 20ms CPU/s in each client at that rate, about 2% of one core; real rule complexity must be bounded. For 500,000 connected sockets, a benchmarked 20,000 sockets per relay suggests twenty-five active relays before spare capacity. I would measure reconnect storms and propagation tail rather than only average fanout.
references.data:
An environment snapshot contains schema version, monotonically increasing configuration revision, typed flag definitions, prerequisites, default values and a content hash/signature. I publish revisions as immutable objects and store an active pointer in a transactional control database. Rule validation rejects cycles, incompatible types and unbounded expensive expressions before publication.

Percentage rollout uses a fixed algorithm such as SHA-256 over `environment + flag_id + rollout_salt + subject_key`, mapped to 10,000 buckets. The salt and subject identity stay stable as percentage changes, so expanding 10% to 20% retains the original cohort. I specify byte encoding and hash extraction identically across SDK languages and use shared test vectors.

The SDK atomically swaps whole snapshots and rejects lower revisions. Deltas declare their base revision; a missing base triggers full snapshot fetch. Last-known-good snapshots persist on disk with integrity checks. Safety permission uses a separately validated signed capability with feature ID, revision and expiry, so a malformed ordinary rule cannot bypass its local fail-safe. Secret values live in a separate credential service with appropriate server/client boundaries.
references.flow:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
 O["Flag operator"] -->|author change| A["Control API"]
 A -->|schema and rule checks| V["Validator"]
 V -->|commit revision and audit| D["Control database"]
 D -->|immutable snapshot| S["Snapshot storage"]
 D -->|revision event| P["Distribution relays"]
 P -->|scoped push delta| K["SDK updater"]
 K -->|gap recovery poll| S
 K -->|validated atomic swap| L["Local snapshot"]
 L -->|stable subject bucket| E["Local evaluator"]
 E -->|typed result| C["Application code"]
 H["Safety capability issuer"] -->|bounded enable lease| K
```

Whiteboard walkthrough: I draw the control plane above the local evaluation path. The application arrow ends at local memory, with no control-plane dependency. I add push and polling to the updater, then the safety capability as a separate input. That lets me explain why ordinary stale configuration can stay useful while an expired safety permission disables a risky feature.

`PATCH /environments/prod/flags/f7` with expected revision 81 returns `{revision:82, rollout_state:"staged"}` after validation and audit. Relays send scoped deltas; an SDK at 79 fetches a full snapshot instead of applying a delta based on 81. `evaluate("f7", {user_key:"u9"}, false)` reads one immutable snapshot and returns a typed value plus revision.

A rollout publishes to a small client cohort, compares application health, then expands. Kill-switch disable changes the control revision and pushes urgently to connected clients. Disconnected clients learn nothing new; their independently enforced enable lease expires and they disable locally. Server-side enforcement remains preferable for actions that must never occur after a revocation boundary.
references.failure:
A bad global rule may be syntactically valid but operationally harmful. I would halt rollout on error/latency signals, publish a higher revision containing the previous safe values, and retain last-known-good snapshots. Rolling back by decreasing the revision would be ignored by SDKs. Canarying application behavior is necessary because schema checks cannot predict every business effect.

After twenty-four hours offline, ordinary flags keep their validated cached values under the chosen stale-service contract. Safety-critical enabled features stop when their capability expires. Reconnection sends the current revision; the SDK downloads a full snapshot if deltas were compacted away. A cold client with no valid cache uses embedded typed defaults, not an arbitrary zero value.

A kill switch cannot instantly reach an offline process. I would propose a thirty-second safety lease if the business accepts up to thirty seconds of offline continuation; a five-second lease approaches the propagation target but creates more availability dependence. Expiry checks need a conservative clock strategy that cannot extend a lease on clock rollback or restart. An uncertain clock fails safe. A malformed ordinary snapshot does not replace the validated safety logic.
references.ops:
I would audit actor, environment, reason, expected revision, before/after values and rollout acknowledgements. Propagation reports healthy-connected-client lag and counts disconnected clients separately; treating unreachable clients as 'updated' gives false confidence. SDK metrics include last successful refresh, snapshot revision, evaluation error and safety-lease expiry.

I would validate stable bucketing with cross-language vectors, test out-of-order deltas and restart from a persisted snapshot, and rehearse a twenty-four-hour partition. Control-plane deploys retain backward-compatible schemas until old SDK support is retired. Snapshot distributions are scoped to tenant/environment credentials, and browser-visible flag values are treated as public to that browser.

Secrets use short-lived credentials delivered through an appropriate secret service, never ordinary flag targeting rules. Server credentials inevitably exist in protected process memory during use; I would not claim a rotation mechanism makes them absent from memory. Rollout rollback is a new audited version. Kill-switch drills measure both connected propagation and actual local expiry behavior on an isolated process.

probes.question: How is per-host politeness preserved across workers?
probes.answer: I partition scheduling by canonical host and use one leased, fenced host owner to grant permits across all workers. Its durable row records nextStartAt, concurrency and robots version. URL leases reclaim crashed work but do not enforce host rates. The egress service validates the owner epoch and enforces request spacing before opening connections; failover waits out recorded in-flight permits before granting new ones.

probes.question: How do you canonicalize URLs without merging distinct resources?
probes.answer: I lowercase scheme and host, remove default ports and fragments, and normalize only equivalent URL encodings. I preserve path case, trailing slashes, repeated parameters and query order because those may distinguish resources. A host-specific rule for removing tracking parameters needs evidence and versioning. Redirect aliases and equal body checksums are separate signals, not permission to collapse URL histories. I bound length and parameter count before admitting discoveries.

probes.question: What protects against crawl traps and infinitely generated URLs?
probes.answer: I cap crawl depth, extracted links per page, new URLs per host per day, and total per-host frontier entries. I detect repetitive calendar paths and parameter combinations, quarantine patterns, and let an operator review exceptions. Fetch bytes, decompressed bytes, parse CPU and memory are independently bounded. Deduplication cannot stop infinitely many distinct URLs, so every discovery spends a finite host budget and every retry spends an ordinary fetch permit.

failures.scenario: One domain owns half the frontier.
failures.expected: I give hosts weighted fair scheduling turns with a maximum budget share and reserve capacity for new or overdue hosts. I cap the large domain's admitted discoveries and spill its existing URL rows over storage subshards while preserving one politeness authority. A huge backlog never permits faster origin traffic. I report its deferred coverage and backlog age; other hosts retain scheduling capacity.

failures.scenario: Workers crash after fetching but before recording success.
failures.expected: The expired URL lease makes work reclaimable. I store bodies under checksums and commit metadata by URL/fetchGeneration, conditionally advancing selected content only for the current lease and generation. The metadata transaction writes discovery outbox events before acknowledgment. A retry may repeat the GET but cannot let an old worker overwrite a newer version; duplicates in storage and discovery are idempotent. Retries remain subject to host spacing and backoff.

references.scope:
I would build seed ingestion, a durable URL frontier, host scheduling, bounded HTTP fetching, isolated parsing and extraction, content storage, and recrawl scheduling. My first correctness requirement is that adding workers cannot increase the permitted rate to a host. Robots decisions and request start times belong in the scheduler, before any connection opens. I would use an identifiable crawler user agent and a contact page.

My additional assumptions are public HTTP/HTTPS resources, no authentication, no form submission, and ordinary GET requests only. I would start with HTML and selected text documents. JavaScript execution is out of scope, so client-rendered applications, authenticated pages, and interaction-dependent content will have incomplete coverage. I would make that limitation visible in crawl reports.

POST /crawl/seeds accepts bounded seed batches and a crawl policy; GET /crawl/jobs/{id} reports coverage, backlog age, and exclusions. Customers can request freshness priorities within their budget, but cannot override robots restrictions or host limits. I would reject private-address destinations and revalidate DNS and each redirect target so extraction cannot turn this public crawler into an internal-network fetcher.
references.estimates:
One hundred million fetches per day is 100,000,000 / 86,400, or about 1,157 requests per second sustained. I would provision for an assumed threefold burst, about 3,500 requests per second, while preserving each host's limit. Assuming a two-second mean fetch duration, Little's law gives roughly 2,314 active fetches sustained and 7,000 at peak; slow-host slots need a separate cap.

At an assumed 300 bytes of frontier metadata per URL, one billion URLs require about 300 GB before indexes, replication, and storage overhead; three copies start around 900 GB. At an assumed 100 KB compressed body per fetched page, new raw content is roughly 10 TB per day before duplicate savings. These assumptions need sampling before procurement.

A ten-day sweep is only arithmetic: host limits and recrawls make universal ten-day freshness impossible. I would reserve a configurable share for new hosts, allocate the rest by observed change rate and value, and use weighted fair host queues. A host limited to one request per second gets at most 86,400 fetches daily; extra fleet capacity cannot fix its backlog. I would report overdue long-tail URLs explicitly.
references.data:
I would partition the frontier by canonical host, with storage subshards for unusually large hosts. A host scheduling row contains owner, fencing epoch, lease expiry, nextStartAt, active permits, and robots cache version. One scheduling authority grants that host's slots across every worker; individual URL leases alone do not enforce politeness. Frontier rows keyed by (host, canonicalUrlHash) hold the original URL, priority, nextDueAt, depth, attempt ID, and worker lease.

A URL record retains ETag, Last-Modified, last success, observed change intervals, response status, and selected content checksum. Bodies are immutable objects keyed by SHA-256; multiple URLs can reference one body without conflating their URL histories. Conditional responses update freshness without reparsing unchanged bytes. URL-hash collisions require comparing the canonical URL itself.

I would persist host permits before issuing them and require a current epoch at the egress service that actually opens connections. That service enforces spacing and concurrency and rejects fenced owners. On owner failover, I would wait out recorded in-flight permits before granting replacements. Otherwise an expired scheduler lease could leave old workers still fetching while a new owner doubles the rate.
references.flow:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  A["Seed or due URL"] -->|"claim URL lease"| B["Host owner"]
  B -->|"load policy"| C["Robots decision"]
  C -->|"allowed and eligible"| D["Fenced fetch permit"]
  D -->|"verify epoch and spacing"| E["HTTP egress"]
  E -->|"bounded response"| F["Content checksum"]
  F -->|"isolate parsing"| G["Parser sandbox"]
  G -->|"bounded links"| H["URL normalization"]
  H -->|"budgeted discoveries"| I["Durable frontier"]
  F -->|"body and metadata"| J["Result commit"]
  J -->|"next due time"| I
```

Whiteboard walkthrough: I claim a due URL, then obtain permission from its host owner. I fetch robots.txt using the same host limiter and apply [RFC 9309](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html). A 4xx unavailable response allows crawling under the protocol, though 429 still triggers my host backoff. For a 5xx or network failure I conservatively disallow crawling until policy recovery; I do not relax this after thirty days. I follow at least five robots redirects, cache successful policy for at most 24 hours normally, and support at least the required 500KiB robots parsing limit. Crawl-delay is an optional configured courtesy extension, not an RFC directive.

The egress service enforces a five-second connect deadline, 30-second total deadline, and 5 MB decompressed-body cap. Redirects require the destination host's policy and permit. Parsing has CPU, memory, and link-count limits. I lowercase scheme/host, remove default ports and fragments, and normalize only equivalent encodings; path case, trailing slashes, and query order remain distinct. Site-specific parameter removal needs evidence. Discovery caps depth at 20, links at 1,000 per page, and new URLs per host per day. I commit result metadata and discovery events durably before acknowledging the leased work.

For example, `POST /crawl/seeds` with `{urls:["https://example.org/docs"], policy_id:"public-text"}` returns 202 `{job_id:"crawl7", state:"scheduled"}` after durable frontier insertion. `GET /crawl/jobs/crawl7` returns fetched, deferred, excluded and failed counts plus the oldest due age. Those counts separate lack of crawl budget from an actual fetching failure.
references.failure:
If a worker dies after fetching, its URL lease expires and the job can be retried. I write bodies by checksum and results by (URL, fetchGeneration), then conditionally advance the URL's selected version using its lease and generation. An old worker can upload an orphaned body but cannot replace a newer selected result. An outbox committed with metadata ensures extraction is eventually enqueued, with canonical-URL uniqueness absorbing duplicate delivery. A repeated GET may still reach the origin; exactly-once network fetching is not promised.

I retry transient transport failures and selected 5xx responses at most three times with exponential backoff and jitter. A 429 applies host-wide backoff, honoring Retry-After; retries acquire ordinary host permits and consume budget. Permanent 404s reduce or stop recrawl according to policy.

When one domain owns half the frontier, I bound its storage growth and scheduling share independently. I spill its URL rows across storage partitions while retaining one host politeness authority. Other hosts keep their fair-queue turns. Calendar loops and faceted-search traps trigger pattern budgets, depth limits, and quarantine; distinct URLs alone are insufficient protection. Hard timeouts release fetch slots, and circuit breakers keep a repeatedly failing host from occupying the fleet.
references.ops:
I would persist frontier and host transitions in replicated storage, with a transactional outbox for downstream work. Checkpoints and replay offsets make recovery proportional to changes since the checkpoint, not one billion URLs. At the estimated sustained rate, even three metadata writes per fetch is about 3,500 writes per second, before discovery traffic; I would measure that amplification and batch discoveries without delaying permit durability. Daily snapshots need storage, I/O, and tested restore procedures.

My dashboard shows fetch rate, response bytes, frontier depth and oldest due age, duplicates by URL and content, parser failures, robots exclusions, 429s, and per-host request-start spacing violations. I would alert on any unauthorized fetch, rather than treating it as a normal percentile metric. Permit logs retain host, policy version, epoch, and start time for audits.

Parsers run in disposable resource-limited processes without network access. I would test malformed archives, decompression bombs, runaway link lists, stale owner epochs, and lease failover while connections remain active. Recrawl priority should be evaluated against measured content changes and long-tail coverage so popular sites do not silently monopolize the crawl budget.

probes.question: How do you find nearby drivers without scanning all locations?
probes.answer: I query the pickup cell and neighboring cells through a spatial index, deduplicate driver IDs, discard expired or stale locations, and score a bounded fresh candidate set by distance and ETA. I expand the radius within a time and fanout budget when fresh supply is low. Dense cells split into finer child cells with independently partitioned indexes and a versioned directory. Spatial availability is only a hint; the authoritative reservation transaction checks the driver again.

probes.question: Where does a proposed assignment become authoritative?
probes.answer: The offer becomes an authoritative reservation when one conditional transaction verifies ride=searching and driver=available and writes both records with the same offer ID and expiry. Only a committed outbox event permits offer delivery. Confirmation happens later in an acceptance transaction that checks both versions, matching offer IDs, and the deadline, then assigns both records atomically. Cancellation and timeout use the same authoritative states, so neither can release or accept an unrelated newer offer.

probes.question: What happens when location data is stale?
probes.answer: I keep server receivedAt plus device session and sequence with each point. I reject out-of-order updates and exclude drivers whose location is older than the declared freshness threshold. Device clocks cannot extend that threshold. I request a fresh update and look for other fresh drivers or expand the fresh-candidate search; I do not infer a reliable pickup ETA from old coordinates. Reservation still rechecks authoritative availability because even a fresh point cannot prove the driver is free.

failures.scenario: Two dispatchers offer rides to the same driver.
failures.expected: Both dispatchers must conditionally transact on the driver record together with their ride records. Only one changes available to reserved; the loser chooses another candidate without sending an offer. Acceptance checks the winning offer ID, expiry and both versions. Accept, cancellation and timeout transactions serialize: the first legal commit determines the state, and delayed transitions fail their conditions. An uncertain result is read back using the offer's idempotent ID.

failures.scenario: A dense city cell becomes a hotspot.
failures.expected: I adaptively split the geographic cell into child cells on independent index partitions, publish a versioned directory, and temporarily dual-write/query parent and children while deduplicating driver IDs. Bounded parallel child queries and candidate sampling keep matching latency controlled. A wider radius alone adds work without removing the hotspot. Driver reservation remains authoritative by driver ID in joint ride/driver transactions, so redistributing location entries cannot weaken exclusivity.

references.scope:
I would expose driver location reporting, ride creation, candidate search, offer delivery, accept or reject, rider cancellation, and completion. The hard invariant is that one driver cannot be confirmed for two active rides. A declined or unanswered offer is normal and should move matching forward without leaving ownership ambiguous.

My extra assumptions are authenticated drivers and riders, one authoritative home region per active ride, and an offer deadline of 10 seconds. I interpret the two-second p95 requirement as time to select and durably reserve a candidate and initiate an offer; human acceptance cannot reliably fit that deadline. I would confirm that interpretation with the interviewer and track acceptance separately.

Pricing, route calculation, and payment are outside this service. I consume a quote ID, vehicle eligibility rules, and bounded ETA estimates from those services, then emit confirmed/completed events for charging and trip execution. POST /rides uses a rider-scoped idempotency key; POST /offers/{id}/accept, /reject, and POST /rides/{id}/cancel carry expected versions. Driver location messages carry session ID, sequence, coordinates, and device time.
references.estimates:
The ride peak is 20,000 / 60, about 333 new rides per second. Location ingest is 1,000,000 / 5, or 200,000 updates per second, roughly 600 times larger. At an assumed 150 bytes per location envelope, that is 30 MB per second of payload, before network overhead and replication. Retaining every update would add 2.6 TB per day, so the online index stores only current positions; sampled history is a separate bounded analytics stream.

Assuming 500 bytes per current indexed driver including timestamps and cell membership, one million positions consume about 500 MB logical, with substantial allocator, index, and replica overhead. With an assumed 30% acceptance probability, a simplified independent model gives 1 / 0.3, or 3.3 offers per ride: roughly 1,100 reservations per second. Actual rejection correlations and burst density matter more than that average.

I would budget the first offer path at 100 ms intake, 150 ms cell query, 300 ms bounded scoring/ETA, 150 ms reservation, and 200 ms delivery, leaving about 1.1 seconds for queueing and retries. Scanning one million positions for each request means 333 million position examinations per second and unstable tail latency. Local candidate bounds are essential.
references.data:
I would keep ephemeral locations in a regional spatial index keyed by (cellId, subcellId, driverId), and a latest-location record keyed by driverId. Each carries server receivedAt, device timestamp, session, and sequence. Monotonic sequence checks reject delayed updates; server time bounds freshness without trusting device clocks. With an assumed 15-second freshness threshold, expired drivers disappear from candidate queries even if cleanup lags.

Authoritative regional storage has Driver(driverId, state, rideId, offerId, version, expiresAt), Ride(rideId, state, driverId, offerId, version), and Offer(offerId, rideId, driverId, expiresAt, status). Ride states are searching, offered, assigned, inTrip, completed, or cancelled. Driver states are available, reserved, assigned, or offline. Reservation and acceptance change both records in one conditional transaction. A spatial cache saying available never grants ownership.

I would start with cells sized for urban pickup searches, then adapt density with child cells and a versioned split directory. Smaller cells reduce candidates but increase neighboring-cell fanout. During a split I dual-write locations and query parent plus children, deduplicating driver IDs, until old membership expires. Eligibility and offer ownership remain keyed by driver ID, independent of index reshaping.
references.flow:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  A["Ride API"] -->|"idempotent create"| B["Searching ride"]
  B -->|"pickup and directory"| C["Neighbor cells"]
  C -->|"fresh eligible drivers"| D["Bounded ETA scoring"]
  D -->|"best candidate"| E["Reservation transaction"]
  E -->|"ride and driver committed"| F["Offer outbox"]
  F -->|"offer ID and deadline"| G["Driver device"]
  G -->|"accept current offer"| H["Acceptance transaction"]
  H -->|"commit assignment"| I["Rider confirmation"]
  G -->|"reject or timeout"| J["Conditional release"]
  J -->|"next candidate"| B
```

Whiteboard walkthrough: I create the ride once, query nearby cells, discard stale locations, bound candidate count, and rank using ETA and eligibility. A serializable transaction requires the ride still searching and the driver available, then writes both as reserved/offered with one offer ID and deadline and an outbox event. Only that commit authorizes sending the offer; it reserves a candidate but does not yet confirm a ride.

Acceptance checks authoritative server time, offer ID, both versions, and unexpired reservation, then atomically assigns both ride and driver and writes confirmation events. Cancellation changes the ride and releases the same driver in a conditional transaction. If cancellation commits first, acceptance fails; if acceptance commits first, cancellation rechecks the new version and may atomically cancel the assigned pre-trip ride and release its driver. Once inTrip, the trip service owns cancellation policy. Reject/timeout releases only a matching reservation and returns the ride to searching. Delayed messages cannot release a newer offer.

For example, `POST /rides` with `Idempotency-Key: rider17-trip4` and `{pickup:{lat:37.78, lon:-122.42}, quote_id:"q9"}` returns `{ride_id:"r7", state:"searching"}`. The offer notification carries `{offer_id:"o8", ride_id:"r7", expires_at:"...", version:3}`. An accept returns assigned IDs only after the joint transaction commits; an expired or superseded offer returns 409 and the current authoritative state.
references.failure:
If two dispatchers select one driver, their joint ride/driver reservation transactions compete on the same authoritative driver version. One commits; the loser retries another fresh candidate before sending anything. An uncertain commit result is resolved by reading the idempotent offer ID, rather than blindly creating another offer. Outbox redelivery may duplicate a notification, which devices deduplicate by offer ID.

A stale location is excluded. I do not widen the radius and treat an old coordinate as trustworthy; I can request a fresh update and search additional fresh candidates. Availability changes between index read and reservation are caught by the transaction. A driver losing connectivity after reservation times out; acceptance arriving after the deadline fails even if the cleanup job has not yet run.

For a dense concert pickup cell, I split into finer geographic children with independent index partitions and bounded parallel queries. A versioned directory and overlap period prevent missing drivers during migration. Candidate sampling and per-cell query budgets bound fanout, sacrificing optimality explicitly when needed.

During authoritative-store failure, I stop confirming assignments in that region. Cached candidates cannot preserve exclusivity. Recovery replays committed outbox events and conditionally expires old offers; regional failover requires fencing the former writer before another region can accept transitions.
references.ops:
I would measure time to first offer, time to acceptance, acceptance/rejection/timeout rates, reservation contention, stale-location exclusions, candidate counts, query fanout, and outbox lag. Wait-time percentiles by pickup area and time of day reveal neighborhoods harmed by a global latency target. I would also track assignment invariant violations, which should be zero, and location ingest lag separately from matcher latency.

I would route drivers and rides to a regional authority using a stable home-region token. I assign only drivers whose authoritative region matches the ride, so the same regional transaction can update both records. Neighboring location indexes are advisory for supply planning, not permission to reserve a driver owned elsewhere. Moving an available driver between regions requires an explicitly fenced ownership transfer: the old authority disables reservation, the destination imports the available driver record, and a committed ownership change permits new reservations only after the former owner is fenced. The driver cannot be assigned in either region during transfer and cannot transfer with an active ride. An active ride stays in its original region. This reduces usable supply near boundaries and during failures, which I would explain as the cost of preserving exclusivity without a cross-region transaction.

My declared product choice is a bounded fresh-candidate set and fast first offer over an exhaustive globally optimal match. I would compare pickup ETA, abandonment, and geographic fairness before reducing search work. Load tests should include synchronized location bursts, cell splits, accept/cancel races, delayed acknowledgments, and database failover; average request throughput alone cannot validate the service.

probes.question: How do you know a rendition is complete and safe to serve before the transcode finishes?
probes.answer: I never trust a status flag. Each rung is encoded into a staging prefix and a verifier checks three things before promoting it: the expected segment count is present, the sum of segment durations matches the container probe within a tolerance, and every segment carries a checksum the edge can re-check on read. Until that passes, the manifest version does not reference the rung at all, so the rung is unreachable rather than half-reachable. If two rungs of five pass, I publish the ladder that passed and record the missing rung on the video record, because a partial ladder that a player can see degrades adaptively; a partial ladder it cannot see does not exist. A re-run writes the same `(rendition_id, segment_index)` keys, so retry is idempotent.

probes.question: Trace a play request from a player in Frankfurt to its first video frame, naming every hop and every cache it consults.
probes.answer: The player asks for `/videos/v1/manifest` with a playback token scoped to that video. The Frankfurt edge answers from cache if it can, otherwise it fetches the published manifest version from the manifest store and caches it keyed by that version, so a republish cannot pair a new rung list with old segments. The client measures throughput on the first segments, picks 720p or 1080p, and requests segments by URL from the manifest. Those go to the same edge: cache hit returns bytes directly, a miss goes to the object store and is filled on the way back. First frame therefore costs one edge lookup on a warm rung and two on a cold one. Token minting is a separate short call to the token service; I would cache the token in the player for minutes rather than mint per segment.

probes.question: A transcode worker dies 40% of the way through the 1080p rendition. What does the player see, and is the retry safe?
probes.answer: Nothing, if publish is gated on verification: the 1080p rung never entered a manifest version, so no player ever held a URL for a segment that does not exist. Players on other rungs are unaffected. The retry is safe because segments are keyed by `(rendition_id, segment_index)`, so re-encoding writes the same keys and a duplicate segment is the same object; I do not need exactly-once encoder work, I need idempotent output. Two things would make it unsafe: promoting on the transcoder's own success callback instead of the verifier, which publishes a truncated tail, and letting the retry use a different encoder version, which mixes codecs inside one ladder. I pin the encoder version per rung, and a rung that fails verification twice is dropped from the ladder and recorded on the video rather than blocking the whole publish.

failures.scenario: One video reaches 20,000 concurrent viewers within an hour of upload.
failures.expected: I do the arithmetic on the single object first: 20,000 concurrent viewers x 2.5Mbit/s = 50,000Mbit/s = 50Gbit/s = 62.5GB/s, and at a 5% edge miss rate the origin still absorbs about 3.1GB/s from one key, which is a hot-key problem before it is a bandwidth problem. Segment demand is 20,000 / 4s = 5,000 requests/s on one rendition prefix, so the token service would also become a hot key unless tokens are scoped per session and reused for minutes. Three responses: pre-warm the ladder into the edge as soon as the video is published rather than waiting for demand, cap per-object origin rate so one key cannot evict the catalog, and make sure the ladder is complete before announcing the video, because a viral 1080p 404 costs more trust than a delayed publish. I would hold a per-video concurrency budget and shape above it rather than let the edge decide.

failures.scenario: The origin region for Asia-Pacific is unreachable for 20 minutes.
failures.expected: Playback of anything already cached continues, because most bytes come from the edge and the edge does not need the origin region. The exposure is first requests: a manifest miss needs the manifest store, so I run that multi-region with a documented staleness bound rather than relying on the regional primary. What I refuse to do is silently cross-region re-origin at peak: at 25% of traffic, Asia-Pacific is about 125Gbit/s of client egress and even a 5% miss rate is 6.25MB/s pulled over an inter-region link, which costs more than the outage and can cascade into the other region. Cold-start playback in Asia-Pacific degrades to a slower first frame and a lower chosen rung for the duration, and I would tell the interviewer that honestly rather than promise the 1 second target. On recovery the region drains its cache-fill backlog rather than re-priming eagerly, so it does not stampede a region that was serving fine.

references.scope:
I would split this into five operations, because the interviewer usually wants to collapse them into one: upload the master, transcode the ladder, publish, fetch the manifest, fetch segments. A creator's upload returns a video ID immediately and nothing is playable yet. Publishing is a separate step that makes that ID resolvable to players. Playback is a manifest fetch plus a long series of segment requests, and adaptive bitrate means the client picks from the options we offer rather than from one URL we chose for it.

The two jobs pull against each other. On the write side a new video should be watchable in minutes, and transcoder time is both the cost and the constraint. On the read side, time to first frame under 1 second from Sao Paulo means most requests never reach us at all, which is a cost decision as much as a latency one. Nothing about the write path is per-request interactive; nothing about the read path is per-request authoring.

Out of scope: live streams, because a sliding-window manifest and continuous ingest break both publish-after-ladder and any completeness check; DRM, because it inserts a license service between the manifest and the keys and changes the caching story; and encoder internals, which are given to me. Author analytics and recommendations are also out, since neither is on the critical path and both would pull the interview off the bytes. If paywalls come up, the signed manifest URL is where they belong, not the segment bytes. I would also say out loud that a video is not deleted by hiding a row: erasure has to reach the master, every rung, every cached copy we can invalidate, and the edge, which is a different and much harder promise than playback stopping.
references.estimates:
Upload first. 10,000 masters/day at 20 minutes and 8Mbit/s is 1,200s x 8,000,000bit/s = 9.6e9 bits = 1.2GB per master, so 12TB/day. That is 12TB / 86,400 = 139MB/s averaged over the day, and I would size ingest for a 10x evening peak at roughly 1.4GB/s, which is the argument for presigned direct-to-storage uploads. Proxying 1.4GB/s through the API tier buys nothing and makes the API tier a bandwidth failure domain.

The ladder is the second number. Five renditions summing to about 8.7Mbit/s against an 8Mbit/s master means the ladder writes roughly what it reads, so about 12TB/day of encode output, which is 1.1Gbit/s sustained. I will assume one encoder node emits 100Mbit/s of encoded output until I measure it on our own codec and rung sizes; 1,111Mbit/s / 100Mbit/s = 11 nodes, and I would run 16 with room for re-encodes and peaks. That 100Mbit/s is an assumption to benchmark, not a specification, and if it measures 50Mbit/s the fleet doubles and publish latency doubles with it. Encoder capacity is the resource that constrains publish latency first, because storage and egress are elastic and encoder nodes are not.

Playback is where the money is. 200,000 concurrent viewers at an assumed 2.5Mbit/s average selected rendition is 200,000 x 2.5Mbit/s = 500,000Mbit/s = 500Gbit/s = 62.5GB/s at peak. Peak concurrency sizes capacity; average concurrency sizes the bill. Assuming average concurrency runs at a tenth of peak, 20,000, sessions/day are 20,000 x 86,400 / 1,200 = 1.44 million, and 1.44 million x 1,200s x 2.5Mbit/s = 4.32e15 bits = 540TB/day, about 16PB/month of client egress. At a 95% edge hit rate the origin sees 5% of that, roughly 800TB/month. Segment requests at a 4-second segment are 200,000 / 4 = 50,000/s at peak, nearly all edge hits. Storage is modest beside that: masters plus ladder at two replicas is 48TB/day, about 17.5PB a year, and the ladder is the part worth tiering after 30 days. Egress, not storage and not transcoding, is the first thing I would optimise.
references.data:
I would keep the entities separate, because they have different lifetimes and different keys.

Video is identity and lifecycle: ID, owner, master object key, probed duration, state (uploaded, transcoding, published, failed), and which manifest version is currently published. Rendition is one rung of the ladder, keyed `(video_id, rendition_id)`, holding width, height, bitrate, codec, segment duration, encoder version, expected segment count and a verification result. Manifest version is immutable once written: it lists the ladder and the segment templates for one publish, so a republish is a new version rather than an edit in place. Playback session is ephemeral, keyed by the playback token, holding the chosen rung and last segment served. Watch position is durable and per device, so a viewer resumes on a different handset. Segment is addressed by `(rendition_id, segment_index)` and never by a URL that embeds a timestamp.

Completeness is the part I would not leave to a status flag. A rung becomes servable only after a verifier confirms the expected segment count, that summed segment durations match the probe within a tolerance, and that each segment carries a checksum. Until then the manifest version does not reference it. Publish is therefore gated on the ladder, and a rung that fails twice is dropped from the ladder and recorded on the video rather than blocking the whole publish.

Because segments are keyed by rendition and index, re-running a transcode writes the same keys and the retry is idempotent; I do not need exactly-once encoder work, only deterministic output. A master re-uploaded under the same ID must create a new video version, or old manifests would point at new bytes. The signed playback token is not an entity; it is a short-lived scope derived from an entitlement, and it carries no state I need to store.
references.flow:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
 P["Player in Frankfurt"] -->|manifest and segments| E["CDN edge"]
 E -->|cache hit| P
 E -->|segment miss| O["Object store"]
 O -->|segment bytes| E
 E -->|manifest miss| M["Manifest store"]
 M -->|published rung list| E
 U["Creator"] -->|presigned PUT| O
 O -->|master landed| Q["Transcode queue"]
 Q -->|one rung encoded| T["Staging prefix"]
 T -->|count, duration, checksum verified| M
 M -->|new manifest version| E
 S["Playback token service"] -->|short-lived scope| E
```

Whiteboard walkthrough: the edge is the only component every request touches, so it goes in the middle with the manifest store and the object store behind it. The publish path is the interesting one, so I draw it separately: upload lands as an object, a queue claims it, each rung is encoded into staging, a verifier promotes the rung, and only then does a new manifest version exist. I keep the segment path and the manifest path on separate arrows because a warm manifest and a cold segment are different problems.

`GET /videos/v1/manifest` with a token scoped to that video returns the published manifest version: the rung list with widths, bitrates and a segment template each. The player measures throughput on the first segments and picks a rung; a seek is a range request against the same manifest, not a new session. A manifest miss goes to the manifest store, and the response is cached at the edge keyed by manifest version, so a republish cannot serve a stale rung list against new segments. A segment miss goes to the object store and is filled on the way back, which is the only path that crosses an ocean.

`POST /videos/v1/upload` returns presigned PUT URLs straight to storage. When the last rung verifies, the publisher writes a new immutable manifest version and flips the video's published pointer. Before that, the manifest returns not-playable-yet, and the creator's own preview is served from the staging prefix under a creator-scoped token, so preview never needs the publish path to be complete.
