Losing the Asia-Pacific origin region is a first-request problem, not a playback problem. Anything the edge holds keeps playing, because most bytes come from the edge and the edge does not depend on that region. Manifest misses need the manifest store, so I run that multi-region with a stated staleness bound rather than trusting a regional primary. What I refuse to do is silently cross-region re-origin at peak: at 25% of 500Gbit/s, Asia-Pacific is about 125Gbit/s of client egress, and even a 5% miss rate is 6.25Gbit/s, roughly 780MB/s, dragged over an inter-region link, which costs more than the outage and can cascade. Cold-start playback in that region degrades to a slower first frame and a lower chosen rung, and I would say that to the interviewer rather than promise the 1 second target.

A viral video is a hot-key problem. 20,000 concurrent viewers on one object is 20,000 x 2.5Mbit/s = 50,000Mbit/s = 50Gbit/s = 62.5GB/s, and at a 5% miss rate the origin still takes about 3.1GB/s from one key. Segment demand is 20,000 / 4s = 5,000 requests/s on one prefix, so the token service becomes a hot key too unless tokens are scoped per session and reused. I pre-warm the ladder into the edge at publish time, cap per-object origin rate so one key cannot evict the catalog, and hold a per-video concurrency budget that the edge honours by shaping rather than by dropping.

A crashed transcoder is the boring case and it must be boring: idempotent retry on the same segment keys, encoder version pinned per rung, publish still gated on the verifier. A player never sees a truncated tail because the rung was never in a manifest.

The tradeoff I accepted is publish-after-complete-ladder, which costs write-path latency, over publish-early-and-fill-in, which costs player trust on every 404. I would revisit it if upload-to-playable p95 exceeds a threshold I set against creator expectations, or if the ladder itself got much wider; I would not revisit it because one video went viral.
references.ops:
I would report time to first frame at p50 and p95 by region, then rebuffer ratio, then start-up delay per rung, because a cold edge cache and a cold encoder produce the same player symptom from opposite ends. Segment 404 rate per rendition is the metric that distinguishes them: high start-up delay with a low 404 rate is the encoder queue, high start-up delay with a 404 rate spike is the ladder or the manifest. Cache hit ratio belongs on a dashboard split by rung and region, because a rung that is unpopular is fine while a rung that is popular and missing is a bug in pre-warming. Upload-to-playable latency is the write path's own objective, and encode queue age is the leading indicator for it.

A ladder change is a rollout problem. The encoder version is recorded per rung and the manifest version carries the rung set, so a new encoder produces a new rung set rather than overwriting segments a player may still be reading. I canary on a share of new uploads, compare TTFF, rebuffer ratio and segment errors between rung sets, and roll back by stopping the canary, which is a routing decision rather than a data migration. Rungs are never renamed in place.

The security concern that matters most is the signed URL, because it is the only thing between a video and anyone who guesses a path. Tokens are short-lived, scoped to one video and one session rather than a prefix, rate-limited per token, and minted only after an entitlement check, so the manifest URL is also where paywall and geo policy live. Upload validation is the second concern: masters are probed, size and duration capped, and a file that is not the declared container is rejected before it can occupy the encoder fleet, because transcoding is the expensive thing here to abuse.

probes.question: Two engineers push to the same branch seconds apart. What happens to the first run?
probes.answer: Every branch ref has a concurrency group with a monotonic epoch. The second push bumps that epoch, so any queued job from the first run is dropped before it starts rather than queued behind the new one. A job already running gets a cancel that takes effect at the next step boundary. Anything it uploaded goes to quarantine, because a partially uploaded artifact and a good one must not look the same to a consumer. Superseding stops work; it does not undo a deployment the old run already wrote, because reversing that means redeploying a digest I still hold, which is a separate deliberate operation.

probes.question: How does a built image get from a workflow step to a deployment with no shared filesystem?
probes.answer: Artifacts are immutable, content-addressed blobs. The producing job uploads bytes once and gets a sha256 digest back; writing the same artifact key with different bytes is an error, not an overwrite. The run records the digest, and a consuming job or environment pulls that exact digest from object storage or the registry. The orchestration plane only ever carries pointers, never payloads. This is also what makes promotion reproducible: the deployment record references a digest rather than a run, so moving an artifact from staging to production is a pointer change over bytes that were already tested.

probes.question: A step in a fork pull request needs a secret. How do you scope it?
probes.answer: It does not get one. Secrets are issued per job by a token exchange bound to repository, ref and environment, valid for minutes, so a long-lived credential never sits on a machine that ran untrusted code. A fork pull request is untrusted by definition, so it is issued nothing and gets a restricted network profile. On the trusted path, masking happens in the log pipeline rather than trusting the step not to print the value, and egress is default-deny through an allowlisting proxy, so a grant that does leak has nowhere to go. Every grant is recorded with its run and job for audit, and provider-side revocation caps the exposure window.

failures.scenario: A base image change drops the warm cache hit rate from 80% to 5%.
failures.expected: Mean duration goes from 408s to 0.05 x 240 + 0.95 x 1,080 = 1,038s = 17.3 minutes. That needs 0.7 x 1,038 = 727 concurrent runners against 408 planned. Work-conserving throughput at 408 runners is 408 / 1,038 = 0.393 builds/s, so the queue grows by 0.7 - 0.393 = 0.307 builds/s: about 368 jobs of backlog every 20 minutes, and a fast-lane job that used to start in seconds now waits behind them. This is expected rather than broken, because the cache key contains the base image digest and a digest change is a different key. I shed the fast lane to a smaller pool, pre-warm the fleet, and reserve the gated lane's runners so releases still ship while fast feedback degrades. The warm-cache ratio moving is a page, because it predicts queue age before queue age exists.

failures.scenario: A transitive dependency is compromised and every pipeline installs it.
failures.expected: Pin lock files and base images by digest and install without a resolution step, so the dependency is a specific hash rather than a name. When the advisory names that hash I block it at the registry pull path and at the egress proxy, invalidate every cache key containing it, and identify affected runs by digest instead of by guessing. Deployments from the affected window are held rather than assumed clean, and the fast lane is allowed to keep failing loudly, which is the correct outcome here. I also audit which jobs drew a credential grant after the advisory timestamp, because that is where exfiltration would actually appear.

references.scope:
I would frame this as one trigger and two products. One answers every push quickly: lint, unit tests, a build. The other decides what production runs: the same artifacts, plus staging, a human approval and a promotion. Sharing a trigger is cheap. Sharing a lane is what breaks, so the fast lane and the gated lane get separate queues, separate runner pools and separate latency targets.

The operations are registering a workflow definition in a repository, accepting a push, building the workflow graph for that commit, scheduling jobs, streaming logs, fetching artifacts and deploying. A human also re-runs a failed job, cancels a run, or promotes an already-built artifact to another environment. Promotion is the one worth naming explicitly: deploying a stored artifact by digest is what makes a release reproducible rather than hopeful.

Three things are out of scope, and I say so rather than implying I built them. The git host: I consume push events and the commit sha. The container registry internals: I consume an addressable immutable digest. And self-hosted build machines that engineering teams configure themselves, because a runner that executes repository code is the sharpest edge in this system and I do not want it quietly optional. Compiler and test framework internals are also out; the platform treats a step as a command with an exit code.

One decision belongs here rather than in the architecture: a workflow definition is read at the commit sha that was pushed, never at the branch head. Reading the head means the graph that runs is not the graph anyone committed, and every re-run becomes unreproducible.
references.estimates:
10,000 pushes/day is 10,000 / 86,400 = 0.116/s. Eighty percent land in a 10-hour working day, which is 8,000 / 36,000 = 0.22/s, and the intra-day peak is about 5x that, so I size for 1 push/s. Thirty percent are documentation-only and never take a runner, so peak full builds are 1 x 0.7 = 0.7/s. The arrival rate is trivially small. Nothing here is throughput-bound, and a design that spends its budget on request rate has already misread the problem.

Runtime is what matters. A warm build is 4 minutes = 240s and a cold build is 18 minutes = 1,080s. At an assumed 80% warm hit rate, mean job duration is 0.8 x 240 + 0.2 x 1,080 = 192 + 216 = 408s = 6.8 minutes. Concurrent slots needed at peak is 0.7 x 408 = 285.6, so about 286 concurrent runners, and at a 70% target utilization to absorb cold-start jitter that is about 286 / 0.7 = 408 provisioned runners. A 12-step workflow fans its jobs out in parallel, so a single run occupies only a few slots at a time; demand comes from concurrent runs, not from step count. The 408 figure is an assumption to measure, not a number to purchase.

The thing that saturates first is runner slots, and the symptom is queue age rather than error rate. Push throughput will look perfect while a fast-lane job waits eight minutes for a warm slot, which is why I put queue age on the wall rather than in a weekly dashboard.

Storage: 10,000 x 0.7 = 7,000 full builds a day at an assumed 200MB of retained image each is 1.4TB/day, so 14-day artifact retention is about 19.6TB. Logs at an assumed 2MB per run and 10,000 runs a day is 20GB/day, so 30 days is 600GB. Artifacts are the expensive half and expire first.
references.data:
Six entities, and the split between them is what makes resume, audit and cleanup tractable.

A workflow definition is keyed `(repo_id, path, revision)` where revision is a commit sha. A run is keyed `(repo_id, run_number)`, with a unique `(repo_id, commit_sha, workflow_revision, attempt)` so a redelivered webhook cannot create a second run of the same thing. A job is `(run_id, job_key)` carrying state, required runner labels, its concurrency group and a lease epoch. A step attempt is `(job_id, attempt_number)` with start, end and exit code. An artifact is `(run_id, artifact_key)` pointing at an immutable blob plus its sha256 digest and a retention expiry. A log is `(job_id, attempt, seq)`, appended to a stream and never rewritten.

Two decisions are load-bearing. Artifacts are immutable and content-addressed: writing the same key twice with different bytes is an error rather than an overwrite, and a digest is the only handle anything downstream is ever given. Logs are append-only and cheap while artifacts are expensive and expire on a declared policy; conflating them means either losing logs or paying for images forever.

A deployment record references `(environment, artifact_digest, source_run_id, approver)`. It does not reference a run, because a run can be superseded after it deploys and because one artifact may legitimately be promoted to several environments. Credentials are not fields on any of these rows: a grant is its own record `(run_id, job_id, secret_name, issued_at, expires_at)` in an audit log.

Queued work, cache manifests and runner fleet membership are derived state, rebuildable from the runs and the definitions.
references.flow:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
 G["Git host"] -->|push event with delivery id| T["Trigger service"]
 T -->|verify signature, dedupe| R["Run store"]
 R -->|workflow at pushed sha| P["Workflow planner"]
 P -->|ready job set| S["Job scheduler"]
 S -->|claim with lease epoch| O["Orchestrator"]
 O -->|fresh ephemeral runner| X["Isolated runner"]
 X -->|append log chunks| L["Log stream"]
 X -->|immutable artifact plus digest| A["Artifact store"]
 X -->|conditional completion| R
 A -->|pull by digest| D["Deploy job"]
 D -->|approval record| E["Environment"]
 E -->|deployment row| Q["Deployment record"]
 S -->|stale group epoch, cancel| X
```

Whiteboard walkthrough: I draw the trigger on the left and mark the run store as the only place a push becomes accepted. The planner sits next to it because the graph comes from the pushed sha, not the branch head. Then I draw the scheduler with a lease arrow back to the run store, and I draw the runner inside a dashed box with exactly two arrows leaving it: logs out and artifact out. If a third arrow could carry state between jobs, the isolation argument is broken, and I say that out loud. The deploy job reads the artifact store by digest; it never re-runs the build, which is what makes promotion cheap and releases reproducible.

`POST /hooks/push` arrives with a delivery id and an HMAC signature. I verify the signature, dedupe on delivery id, then commit the run row and its first ready job set in one transaction before returning 202. `GET /runs/{id}/logs?job=build&since=0` streams log chunks, and a client that loses its socket reconnects with the last sequence it saw rather than re-reading from the start.

The non-obvious path is the second push to a branch. Each ref has a concurrency group with a monotonic epoch; a new push increments it, stale queued jobs are dropped before they start, and a running job is cancelled at its next step boundary. Its artifacts go to quarantine, because a partial upload must not be indistinguishable from a real one. Superseding is not rollback: if that run already passed its deploy step it wrote a deployment record, and reversing it is a redeploy of a digest I still hold.
references.failure:
The isolation story is the failure story here, so I lead with it. A runner executes whatever the repository's workflow says, and a workflow file is arbitrary code from the platform's point of view. So: one fresh ephemeral runner per job attempt, destroyed when the job ends, with no filesystem, image layer or credential carried over from the previous job. No host mounts, no container socket. Network egress is default-deny through a filtering proxy with an allowlist, including DNS, so a job cannot resolve its way around the policy or reach a cloud metadata endpoint or an internal service address. Credentials are minted per job by a token exchange scoped to repository, ref and environment and valid for minutes; a fork pull request gets none at all. A runner that has run repository code is tainted and disposable, not a machine you wipe and return to the pool.

The poisoned dependency is the case that hurts. Lock files pinned by digest and installed without a resolution step, base images pinned by digest, so the dependency is a specific hash rather than a name. When an advisory names it I block that digest at the registry pull path and the egress proxy, invalidate every cache key containing it, and identify the affected runs by digest instead of by guessing. Deployments from that window are held rather than assumed clean. I audit which jobs drew a credential grant after the advisory timestamp, because that is where exfiltration would appear.

The cache failure is arithmetic. If the warm hit rate falls from 80% to 5%, mean duration becomes 0.05 x 240 + 0.95 x 1,080 = 12 + 1,026 = 1,038s = 17.3 minutes, which needs 0.7 x 1,038 = 727 concurrent runners against 408 planned. Work-conserving throughput at 408 runners is 408 / 1,038 = 0.393 builds/s, so a queue growing at 0.7 arrivals/s against 0.393 departures/s accumulates 0.307 builds/s, about 368 jobs every 20 minutes. A 7-minute feedback loop becomes 25 minutes or worse, and nothing in the error rate moves. I shed the fast lane to a smaller pool, pre-warm the fleet, and keep the gated lane's runners reserved so releases still ship while fast feedback degrades. The warm-cache ratio moving is a page, not a dashboard line, because it predicts queue age before queue age exists.

A runner lost mid-job fails its lease, retries as a new attempt number, and quarantines whatever the dead attempt uploaded. A cancelled run is not rolled back; only a deployment record can be reversed, and only to a digest I still hold.
references.ops:
I would alert on queue age by lane, because that is the number a developer actually feels. Then cold-start time to first log line, the warm versus cold cache ratio, runner pool utilization, run duration distribution by workflow, the share of runs cancelled as superseded, artifact upload and download latency, and any artifact digest mismatch, which is a security signal rather than a performance one. At the business level I would keep deployment lead time from push to production, and its inverse, change failure rate, in front of the team.

Rolling out a change to the platform has two separate paths. Workflow definitions change in the repository and are versioned by the commit that carries them; a pushed workflow is validated for graph validity, unknown runner labels and secret references at push time, not discovered during a run at 2am. The runner fleet itself is upgraded by canary on roughly 5% of the pool, comparing job success rate and cold-start time against the current image before widening. A change to the deploy step itself canaries by environment.

The security concern that matters most is that the runner is where untrusted code meets credentials. I would keep self-hosted runners disposable, ephemeral and on a fleet with no route to anything trusted, alert on a job requesting a secret grant it has never requested before, and pin digests referenced by live deployments so a rollback redeploys bytes I still hold rather than rebuilding code I no longer have. Retention is split on purpose: logs are cheap and kept long enough to debug a deploy, artifacts are expensive and expire on the declared policy.

probes.question: How wide may the rating band get before a pairing stops being fair?
probes.answer: Width is a declared policy, not something I derive, and I publish the schedule in the queue response so the estimate is honest. At the peak a 100-point band holds about 20,000 of the 400,000 online players and the whole queue holds 20,000 tickets, so ordinary bands pair inside one matcher tick and width costs nothing there. I widen by 50 points every 15 seconds of wait, then to 100, then 200, then 400, and past 400 I stop widening and offer an explicit choice. Past about 400 points the gap exceeds the resolution my rating actually has at that level, so the game moves both players' ratings in a direction neither of them earned.

probes.question: A player reconnects 40 seconds after dropping, and the opponent has moved twice. What does that client receive?
probes.answer: It sends `since_ply` with the last ply it acknowledged. The response carries the materialised position, the move list from that ply onward, the authoritative clock after 40 seconds of server-measured downtime, and the last committed ply. Because the server assigns ply, the client can tell whether its own last submitted move landed instead of guessing from local state. It then re-authenticates, which bumps its session epoch, and attaches to the live stream; the older connection is demoted to read-only and closed.

probes.question: How do you detect a player who is not generating their own moves?
probes.answer: Server-side legality is the floor and it is not sufficient, because engine-assisted moves are legal moves. Above the floor I treat detection as evidence, not verdict: move-time distribution against that account's own baseline, agreement with engine lines across many games rather than one, accuracy far above the account's rating, and one account sitting in two games at once. A flagged game has its rating change held pending human review. I do not auto-ban from a single signal, because the penalty lands on the honest opponent whose rating is being rewritten too.

failures.scenario: A player's connection drops mid-game for 90 seconds while their clock keeps running.
failures.expected: The server marks the game disconnected and the clock keeps running, because a clock that stops when you close a laptop is not a clock. Both players see the state and a reconnect grace window. On reconnect the client replays from its last acknowledged ply, and the 90 seconds is charged from server receive timestamps regardless of what the client claims: a client reporting a lower remaining clock is ignored, a client reporting a higher one is a signal rather than a credit. If the player does not return before their flag falls, the server ends the game on time with a reason code and the clock log that proves it, so the opponent never wins a claim they had to be trusted to make. The result posts as an ordinary timeout loss.

failures.scenario: Matchmaking starves in the top two rating bands for 20 minutes on a Saturday night.
failures.expected: The widest band at the top holds under 2,000 players, about 1,000 concurrent games, so it completes at most 1,000 / 25 = 40 pairings a minute no matter how wide the search runs. Arrivals at 300 a minute grow that queue by 260 a minute, so twenty minutes of starvation leaves about 5,200 waiting tickets, and no amount of widening creates games that the band does not have players for. I apply the declared widening schedule, then move the tickets to a long-wait pool with a real estimate and an explicit choice of wider band or untimed game. Nobody is silently placed into a game they did not agree to.

references.scope:
I would split this into two systems that meet at exactly one committed record. Matchmaking owns who plays whom; the game service owns legality, ply order, the clock and the result. The join point is the game record itself, created with both players, their rating snapshot and the clock rules in one transaction. If the matcher is down, games in progress keep playing and the queue holds; if the game service is down, the queue stops creating games. Neither outage requires rebuilding the other.

The operations are joining and leaving the queue, being paired, submitting a move, receiving the opponent's move, reading full game state after a reconnect, and receiving a terminal result that updates the rating. Rated and untimed are separate queues, and a rated game requires both players to have asked for one. I would not quietly move someone between queues to improve the numbers.

Out of scope: tournaments and Swiss pairing, puzzles, lessons, commentary, spectator broadcast, and a real engine-grade anti-cheat product. Cheap statistical detection stays in scope, because it changes how much anyone should trust the rating, and the rating is the product. Also out of scope: which process or machine hosts a game. A game must survive losing the process that was running it, so affinity is an implementation detail I never promise.

The contract that makes the rest possible is that the server is the sole authority for legality, ply assignment and the clock. Clients render, predict and speculate, and none of that is authoritative. That single decision turns cheating and clock disputes from a philosophical problem into a bounded one.
references.estimates:
At the peak, 400,000 are online: 20,000 in a queue and 380,000 in games, so about 190,000 games in progress.

Move rate: 190,000 games x 40 moves = 7.6 million moves per game-length, and a game-length is 25 minutes = 1,500s, so about 5 moves/s fleet-wide. Per game that is one move every 1,500 / 40 = 37.5 seconds. 380,000 open connections is the load that matters and 5 moves/s is nothing, so I scale on connections and use moves/s only as a health signal.

The matchmaking arithmetic is the interesting part. 400,000 players spread over 2,000 rating points means a 100-point band holds 5% of the population, about 20,000 players, and the queue holds 20,000 in total. So most bands have as many players in them as the entire queue has tickets, and pairing latency is one matcher tick rather than a search problem. The tails are the exception: the widest 200-point band at each end holds under 2,000 players, about 1,000 games, and that band completes at most 1,000 / 25 = 40 pairings a minute no matter how wide I make the search. Band width cannot fix a band that is too small. Only admission policy can, which is why my fallback is an explicit offer rather than a wider search.

Storage: 190,000 games in progress x (3,600 / 1,500) = about 456,000 games a day, so 456,000 x 40 = 18.2 million moves a day, and at an assumed 200 bytes a move that is 3.6GB/day, roughly 1.3TB a year. The volume matters less than its consequence: a whole game is 40 moves and about 8KB of log, so resume is replaying the entire move list rather than seeking to a cursor. Chess resume is cheap precisely because a game is small, and I would lean on that instead of building checkpointing I do not need.

Against the targets, pairing within 30 seconds and first move on the opponent's board within 5 seconds: at 20,000 tickets and 5 moves/s the matcher has plenty of room. The latency risk is a starved band, not throughput.
references.data:
Six entities.

`player` is keyed by player_id and holds identity, current rating, rating deviation, volatility, an account-age flag and a pointer to the active game. `rating_history` is keyed (player_id, game_id) and is append-only: rating before, rating after, opponent rating, expected score and the k used. That ledger is what makes a rating dispute answerable rather than argumentative. `game` is keyed game_id with both players and colours, variant, clock rules (base_ms, increment_ms), each side's starting clock, state, current ply, side to move, both rating snapshots, and the terminal result with its reason. `move` is keyed (game_id, ply) holding from and to squares, promotion, SAN, clock remaining after the move and the server receive time, with a unique (game_id, client_move_id) so a move retried over a flaky socket cannot be applied twice. `clock` is server-only: side to move, remaining_ms, increment owed, last action time. `queue_ticket` holds rating at join, mode, join time and widening step.

The load-bearing decisions. Ply is assigned by the server, so a client cannot invent order or re-submit at a different ply. client_move_id gives idempotency at the edge, which is the case a reconnect actually hits. The clock is never taken from the client's word; the client sends its own view for display and the server measures elapsed time between its own receive timestamps. Both ratings are copied into the game record at pairing time, so a rating change mid-game cannot retroactively alter a result that was computed against the old numbers.

Positions are derived, not stored: the move list is the source of truth and the position is materialised for validation. With 40-move games a checkpoint is premature. Connections and sessions are ephemeral and may be discarded freely; game, move and rating records are not.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
 C1["Client A"] -->|join rated queue| Q["Queue service"]
 C2["Client B"] -->|join rated queue| Q
 Q -->|longest wait, best in band| M["Matcher"]
 M -->|reserve both tickets, commit game| D["Game and move store"]
 D -->|board, colours, clock| C1
 D -->|board, colours, clock| C2
 C1 -->|move with client_move_id| G["Game service"]
 C2 -->|move with client_move_id| G

 R -->|append rating history| D
 C2 -->|reconnect with since_ply| G
 G -->|replay missed plies, attach live| C2
```

Whiteboard walkthrough: I draw the queue and the matcher, and I mark the matcher as the only component that creates a game. Its entire output is one committed game row with a reservation on both tickets. Then I draw the game service with the move log as the only authority, the clock inside it rather than in either client, and the rating service downstream of a terminal result rather than of the last move. The two fan-out arrows are separate from the commit arrows, because a player losing their socket must not undo anything.

`POST /queue {mode:"rated"}` returns `{ticket_id:"t7", rating:1500, band_points:100, estimated_wait_ms:4000}`. The matcher takes the longest-waiting ticket, picks the best partner inside the band, consumes both tickets atomically, and commits one game carrying both rating snapshots and colours. `POST /games/g3/moves` with `{client_move_id:"m1", from:"e2", to:"e4"}` is validated against the materialised position, checked against side to move, charged against the server clock by measured elapsed time, appended at the next ply, and fanned out. The response returns `{ply:1, clock_ms:594000}` so the mover can reconcile.

The non-obvious path is reconnect. `GET /games/g3/state?since_ply=17` returns the materialised position, the move list from ply 18, the authoritative clock and the last committed ply. Because the server assigns ply, the client can tell whether its own last submission landed: if its move is in the list it was applied, and if the list shows the opponent to move without it, it was rejected and the server says why.
references.failure:
Disconnect is the ordinary case, not the exception, so it gets a policy rather than an exception handler. When a player's socket drops the server marks the game disconnected and the clock keeps running, because a clock that stops when you close your laptop is not a clock. Both players see the state and a reconnect grace window. The reconnect path replays from the client's last acknowledged ply, and the server clock is authoritative, so a 90-second drop costs about 90 seconds of clock no matter what the client claims. A client reporting a lower remaining clock is ignored; a client reporting a higher one is a signal, not a credit.

If the disconnected player does not return before their flag falls, the server itself ends the game on time, with a reason code and the clock log that proves it. The opponent never wins a claim they had to be trusted to make. That result enters the rating ledger as an ordinary timeout loss, which is the point: a disconnection is not something either side gets to argue about afterwards.

Two clients for one account is the same class of problem, so I fence it the same way. Authenticating a connection bumps a session epoch for that player, and only the newest epoch may submit moves for an active game; the older connection is demoted to read-only and closed. This matters because reconnection is precisely how a second client gets attached, and a rule that only exists for the first drop does not survive the second.

Cheating sits in two layers. The floor is server-side legality: I materialise the position and reject an illegal move, so a modified client cannot do anything a legal client could not, and cannot do even that reliably. Detection above the floor is statistical and therefore evidence, not verdict. I flag games where the move-time distribution is unlike the account's own history, where accuracy runs far above its rating, where openings match engine lines at high agreement across many games, or where one account is in two games at once. A flagged game does not post its rating change; the result is held pending review. I do not auto-ban on a single signal, because a false positive punishes the honest opponent whose rating is being rewritten alongside. The response is escalation: a review queue and tighter pairing restrictions for accounts that earn them.

Starvation is handled in matchmaking rather than here, and the rule is that I never silently place someone.
references.ops:
I would chart pairing latency at p50 and p95, wait time distribution by band and mode, the share of pairings that landed inside the declared band, games in progress, moves/s, and the delivery lag between a committed ply and the opponent seeing it. Then disconnect rate, median reconnect time, clock-forfeit rate, and the lag between a terminal result and its rating history row, because a rating a player cannot see is a support ticket.

Rolling out a matchmaking change is the one place I would not trust a live A/B test. Queue dynamics depend on the waiting population, and a live split halves the density on both arms, so I would replay a day of recorded queue tickets through the new matcher offline and compare predicted wait and band fairness against the current one first. Then canary by region or by rating band, keeping the reservation and commit path shared so both arms produce real games rather than simulations. A rating-system change is different in kind: I compute old and new formulas in parallel for weeks, publish the disagreement distribution, and cut over only once it is understood.

Security and abuse: the abuse that matters is rating inflation through alt accounts, smurfs and shared accounts, because the rating is the product and therefore the thing being attacked. New accounts get a provisional rating that converges quickly, device and network signals inform but never auto-ban, and I restrict pairing by account age at the top of the ladder, where inflation is worth the most and detection has the least room to be wrong.

probes.question: The settlement report has no idempotency key. What do you key on so a repeated row cannot be paid out twice?
probes.answer: The network reference alone is not enough, because the same row can reappear in tomorrow's file with an identical reference and no sequence number to tell the two apart. I key a settlement line on the content identity of the row: network reference, business date, gross amount, fee and currency, hashed. That key carries a unique constraint, so a repeat becomes an insert-if-absent that is a no-op and the first line stays on the books. If the same network reference arrives with different content, that is not a duplicate, it is a restatement, and I refuse to overwrite the original; it becomes a correction posting dated when I learned of it. So the identity question answers to what the row said, not what the network called it. I also keep the report file id and line ordinal so an auditor can point at the exact bytes behind any posting.

probes.question: The report states a fee that does not match the fee we charged. What do you do with that line?
probes.answer: I never reconcile by overwriting. The matcher compares the reported gross and fee against what I expected for that transaction and classifies the difference before anything is posted. If the total is right and only the fee differs, I post the network's fee as the authoritative cost, book the difference to a fee-variance account, and alert on variance per thousand transactions. If the gross differs, if the currency is not the one I captured in, or if net does not equal gross minus fee, the line does not enter the ledger at all: it goes to an exception queue with expected and reported values attached, and that seller is blocked from the next payout. Posting a line I cannot explain would let the variance disappear into a balance and become invisible exactly when someone needs it.

probes.question: A dispute arrives three weeks after the transaction settled and the money is already in the seller's account. What happens?
probes.answer: I treat it as two entries, not one. The dispute debits the seller a negative posting dated the day I learn of it, referencing the original transaction and the network's dispute reference, and credits a chargeback reserve account. That posting is appended after the closed period, so the original settlement is untouched and the month still replays to the same figures. If the dispute is won, the reserve is released back to the seller on the next payout run as a positive posting. If the seller has already withdrawn, the negative balance goes to receivable and I collect it under a stated policy rather than netting it silently against the next payout. Whether to claw back or fund the loss is a business decision, and I would expose both numbers rather than pick one inside the design.

failures.scenario: The settlement report arrives with an entire day missing.
failures.expected: A missing day is not a smaller day, so I detect it with a coverage check rather than by noticing a low total. Each report declares the business dates it covers and the row count and gross total per date, and ingestion records the expected coverage. If a declared date has no report after the 48-hour lag plus a stated grace, the payout run for every affected seller is blocked and I alert on the oldest uncovered business date. The arithmetic is what makes it visible: at 400,000 transactions and $16 million of buyer volume a day, one missing day is 400,000 transactions and $16 million unsettled, against about $13 million a day of seller proceeds, so a silent gap is larger than a full day of payouts. Nothing is paid on a partial picture, and the seller sees a stated reconciliation-in-progress state rather than a balance that quietly excludes a day.

failures.scenario: A settlement line references a transaction ID we have never recorded.
failures.expected: I quarantine it rather than posting it or dropping it. The line is stored verbatim with its report file id, line ordinal and content identity, marked unmatched, and it contributes nothing to any balance. I check it against three candidate sources in order: a transaction captured in the same window whose amount and date agree but whose reference we stored differently, a transaction in the window caught by a reference-format change between network versions, and a transaction that genuinely never happened on our side, which would mean either a report for another merchant or a compromised reference. The third case is the one I escalate. Quarantined lines age visibly and block payout for that seller until resolved, and I report the quarantine count and gross value daily so it cannot quietly become a large number.

references.scope:
I would treat the ledger as the product and the transfer partner as a channel. The marketplace charges the buyer, holds the money, allocates the seller's share, absorbs the network's report, and pays out. A buyer sees a checkout, a seller sees a balance, and finance sees a set of books that has to agree with both. Card network mechanics, the buyer-facing checkout experience and seller tax reporting are outside this design.

The invariant I state first is that a seller is paid what is owed, exactly once, and nothing is paid that is not owed. That has two halves which pull against each other, and the pull is the whole problem. A repeated report line that I trust produces a double payment, and a report line I refuse until something else confirms it produces a withheld payment. At the same time the balance a seller sees has to move within seconds of the payment, because a seller who cannot see the money contacts support. Fast display and slow truth are two different products, and the fast one never writes the books.

I also say what a report is allowed to change: nothing. Corrections, fee restatements and disputes arrive as later dated entries against an original transaction, so any past period is reconstructed by replaying the ledger rather than by trusting a summary someone stored. A provisional balance is labelled provisional and carries the watermark of the last posting applied, so a seller can be told honestly how much of it is confirmed.
references.estimates:
Twelve million transactions a month is 400,000 a day, about 4.6/s sustained, and at a $40 average ticket that is $16 million of buyer volume a day and $480 million a month. I take 15% of the ticket, so marketplace fee is 15% x $480 million = $72 million a month. The network takes 2.9% plus 30 cents: 2.9% x $480 million = $13.92 million, plus 30 cents x 12 million = $3.6 million, so $17.52 million. Seller proceeds are $480 million - $72 million - $17.52 million = $390.48 million a month, about $13 million a day. Disputes at 0.5% are 0.5% x $480 million = $2.4 million a month, or 60,000 disputes, and I reserve against that rather than discovering it later.

Across 200,000 sellers the average seller sees 12 million / 200,000 = 60 transactions a month: $2,400 gross, less $360 of marketplace fee, less 2.9% x $2,400 = $69.60, less 30 cents x 60 = $18, which leaves $1,952.40 payable before disputes. That is the number the balance screen has to be right about, and it is small enough per seller that a single dispute matters.

Settlement volume is what sizes the reconciliation path, not checkout. At 400,000 report lines a day and a 48-hour lag, at most 800,000 lines are unreconciled at steady state, and a line that does not match becomes an exception row rather than a dropped one. I assume four postings per transaction, so 12 million x 4 = 48 million postings a month, roughly 69GB a year at an assumed 120 bytes per posting, which is small enough that I shard by seller and business date and do not over-engineer it. The first constraint is not storage: it is unmatched settlement lines per run and payout transfer throughput, because both serialise against a partner I do not control.
references.data:
I keep four entities apart, because they have different keys, different lifetimes and different owners. A transaction is what the buyer did: `(merchant_id, order_id, transaction_id)`, captured amount, currency, integer minor units, authorization time and capture time. A settlement line is what the network said happened: network reference, business date, gross, fee, currency, report file id, line ordinal and the row's content identity. A payout is an instruction to move money: payout id, seller id, amount, destination, idempotency key, state and the provider's own reference. A seller balance is not a row I edit; it is a projection of the ledger at a point in time, rebuilt from postings and compared against a stored watermark.

The ledger is append-only double entry. Every movement is a pair of postings in one currency with a signed integer amount in minor units, and the invariant is that the postings for one movement sum to zero. I never use a binary float for money and I never adjust a balance directly; a balance change is always a posting. That is what makes a disputed month answerable by replay: sum the postings and the seller payable falls out, including the escrow held, the fee variance and the dispute reserve.

A settlement line carries a unique constraint on its content identity, which is a hash of network reference, business date, gross and fee. Re-inserting identical content is a no-op and the first line stands. The same network reference with different content is a restatement, not a duplicate, so it is refused as an update and becomes a correction. Reconciliation tables record match state, expected and reported values and a resolved-by, so an exception is a row with a life cycle rather than a log line.
references.flow:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
 B["Buyer checkout"] -->|authorize and capture| G["Payment gateway"]
 G -->|capture result| T["Transaction record"]
 T -->|balanced postings| L["Double-entry ledger"]
 L -->|projected postings| E["Seller balance"]
 N["Daily settlement report"] -->|file and line| S["Report ingestion"]
 S -->|content identity dedupe| D["Settlement line"]
 D -->|normalized money| M["Settlement matcher"]
 L -->|expected gross and fee| M
 M -->|exact match| P["Posting to ledger"]
 M -->|difference or unknown reference| X["Exception queue"]
 E -->|available balance| O["Payout run"]
 X -->|blocks that seller| O
 O -->|idempotent transfer| V["Transfer partner"]
 P -->|releases the funds| E
```

Whiteboard walkthrough: I draw the checkout writing to the ledger and not to the transfer partner, because the books are mine and the money movement is theirs. I put report ingestion between the file and the matcher with a labelled content-identity step, because that step is what makes a repeated row free. Then I draw the exception queue as the branch that does not reach the ledger, and I make it block the payout run, which is the part people forget.

`POST /charges` with `{order_id:"o1", amount_minor:4000, currency:"USD"}` returns `{transaction_id:"t5", captured:true, provisional_balance_published:true}`. Capture posts buyer debit, escrow credit, seller payable credit and platform revenue debit in one transaction, and the seller balance projection is updated in the same commit so the fast number is never a separate write.

`POST /reports` with `{file_id:"f2026-10-04", covers_business_date:"2026-10-04", row_count:401288, gross_total_minor:1605152000}` ingests lines, rejecting any row whose content identity already exists. The matcher compares gross and fee against the expected settlement for each transaction in the window. An exact match posts and closes the transaction; a fee difference posts the network's figure to a fee-variance account and alerts; anything else lands in the exception queue. The payout run then computes available balance per seller from posted, undisputed, unreconciled funds minus a dispute reserve, refuses any seller with an open exception, and submits an idempotent payout batch whose key is the run id.
references.failure:
A repeated settlement line is the first failure and it is not a rare one, because the network is allowed to resend a day's file. The insert-if-absent on content identity makes it a no-op, so the duplicate costs one round trip and no posting. A line with the same network reference and different content is a restatement: I refuse to update the original settlement line and post a dated correction instead, so the closed day still replays to the figures it was closed with.

A missing day is not a smaller day, so I detect it from coverage rather than from a total that looks low. Each report declares the business dates it covers and the row count and gross per date. After the 48-hour lag plus a stated grace, an uncovered business date blocks the payout run for every affected seller and pages on the oldest gap. The arithmetic is why this deserves an alert: at 400,000 transactions and $16 million a day, one missing day is 400,000 transactions and $16 million unsettled, against roughly $13 million a day of seller proceeds, so a silent gap is larger than a full day of payouts and cannot be absorbed.

A late correction and a dispute are the same mechanism. Both append a dated posting against the original transaction, whether the report is three days late or a dispute is opened three weeks after the money moved. If the seller has already withdrawn, the negative balance becomes a receivable under a stated collection policy rather than an invisible reduction of the next payout.

The tradeoff I accepted is that a seller whose money is genuinely owed can be blocked for days by one unrecognised line. I took it because the alternative, paying out on a partial picture, risks money that cannot be recovered. The signal that would change my mind is a dispute rate high enough that blocking becomes the bigger loss, measured as payout-window overrun per seller; I would then add a bounded risk-based release rather than a general relaxation. I would monitor unreconciled volume and the oldest uncovered business date, exception queue depth split by reason, duplicate line rate, fee variance per thousand transactions, payout failure and return rate, and the gap between the projected seller balance and the ledger for a sampled set of sellers. A daily reconciliation closes the loop with three independent numbers: buyer debits captured, settlement gross reported by the network, and the sum of ledger postings per currency. A break larger than a stated tolerance pages someone rather than waiting for a seller to notice.

Support needs to answer a seller who disputes their balance, so I keep the walk from a payout back to its postings, back to the settlement lines, back to the report file and line ordinal. That is the same trail a regulator would ask for, which is why I would build it once and expose it internally rather than build a second audit tool later.

Rolling out is where a ledger change earns its caution. Money-path changes go behind a feature flag, are replayed over a shadow period against historical reports, and are compared posting by posting before they write anything. The reconciliation job itself is the deployment gate: if the shadow run disagrees by even one cent on any seller, the change does not ship. I would rehearse a duplicate report, a missing day, a report in an unexpected currency and a transfer partner outage with a partial batch accepted.

The security concern that matters most is the ability to move money. The transfer partner's credential is the crown jewel: it is scoped to one account, rotated on a schedule, and held in the secret store with no path to a log line or an export. I also separate the permission to schedule a payout from the permission to release funds, so a compromise of the dashboard cannot move money, and I log every payout initiation with the actor, the run id and the balance snapshot it was computed from. I would test a replayed payout batch, a forged report line and a seller who edits their own payout destination.
